chapter: Funerals, second lines and being an outsider
title: Feeling like an intruder at black neighborhood parades
summary: Wood felt a white stranger in a black neighborhood but was never made unwelcome, and recalls being pulled into a second line.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Uh, there would, there would be drunks at parades. Uh, this one we talked about, uh, over on Hamburg Street. But, uh, I remember there was somebody who was, uh, followed along and got noisy. And, uh, somebody would, you know, get him to go back up on the porch. But pretty soon he'd be back down again yelling. And, uh, he wasn't really disruptive. But I, I, as, I always felt, Dick, whenever, uh, never really got over this. That when we went to those parades, you met, you were a white person going into a black neighborhood. And, uh, you were, in effect, kind of honing in to hear the music that was really there for some other purpose. And I always felt like I was something of, of an intruder. And, uh, I tried to sort of keep a little bit out of the way and not be, you know, a real intruder. Although it was inescapable, you know, that I was, uh, you know, a stranger who was not really a part of the sort of organic functioning of the occasion. But, uh, as, as, as an intruder and an observer, you, I couldn't help but observe that this guy was, uh, he was pretty drunk. But I think I kind of wrote it off. This is a weekend and he's probably celebrating not having to work, uh, whatever. Or, uh, yeah, they were, but on the other hand, you know, even though I was, um, very conscious of being, uh, you know, a stranger and, and an intruder. Although, because we went often enough that, well, I'm sure that we were familiar faces to the musicians. The sponsoring groups didn't really know who we were. And the musicians made us always feel like they were pleased to have us there to hear them play. Uh, and I don't, I've never known, you know, how much of that was a genuine thing or how much of that was just sort of a politeness, uh, on their part. Whether they cared whether you were there or not. I got the impression that they liked having people appreciate their music and that, but, and I would like to think that that was the case. Um, and, but while I felt that sort of strangeness and being an intruder, I never really, uh, was made by anybody to feel unwelcome. I mean, nobody ever said to me, you know, like, white guy, what are you doing here?

Yeah. And, uh, I never felt threatened or menaced in any way at all. Uh, in fact, I remember one day, somewhat to my surprise, uh, having gone to, I believe it was a funeral, and they were playing the warm-up number as they did. They would assemble at some place a couple of three blocks away from where the home was, where the body was, or where the funeral home was. And then they would have a warm-up, play a fast number, go around a block a couple of times. Uh, and that would clear the houses if people just come streaming out onto the streets. Then, and we were kind of bouncing along down the sidewalk, uh, kind of timidly into the second line routine. And all of a sudden, at all of a sudden, at all of a sudden, at all of a sudden, somebody had me by the hand and was pulling me along and, uh, sweeping me up with the whole second line thing. Uh-huh. You know, uh, it was, uh, kind of took me by surprise. And somebody I'd never seen before and probably never saw again. But, uh, it was part of the spectacle. And, uh, it was part of the spectacle.
I was in the midst of it.
